PSI U PERSONALITY OF THE MONTH
Richard Dyer-Bennet, Epsilon '36
By Edward C. Peattie, Phi '06
RICHARD
DYER-BENNET knew, when
he left his San Francisco home nine
years ago, that he was embarking on a
career that had httle to do with the playing
field.
But his home town was
considerably
surprised last season when the Olympic
Club soccer star came home, a concert star
with a
guitar in his arms instead of a foot
ball, an artist with a national reputation.
While he was an
undergraduate at the
University of California, the young San
Franciscan was divided between a career
in Drofessional soccer and the life of a
concert singer, and for a while he thought
he would combine them. His plans were
abruptly changed when, in a
game on
Christmas Day for the Olympic Club, an
opponent hurtled into him and broke his
nose.
Realizing that broken noses are no
aid to good voice production, he reluc
tantly resigned from the sport and devoted
himself to voice study under Mrs. J. W.
Beckman, who heard him at a Christmas
party in the Epsilon house.
Obsei-ving his eager preference for the
songs of the people over the centuries and
a
gift for folksinging, Mrs. Beckman urged
him to journey to Sweden to hear the
ancient troubadour, Sven Scholander.
Equipped with a lute, a
bicycle, and $500
left him by a
person he had never seen,
a thin young man with a sweet tenor voice
set forth from California in search of a
career.
He went to Sweden, where, he had
heard, an old man lived who practiced the
art he meant to learn. The old man
obligingly took dovwi his own lute from a
shelf and sang in the quavery voice of age
some of the songs he had sung to three
generations of Europeans.
"Somehow, it was the greatest musical
experience I ever had," recalls Richard
Dyer-Bennet of that visit to 75-year old
Sven Scholander, the greatest minstrel of
the recent past. It was, for young DyerBennet, a confirmation of his love of the
song stories of the people, the tender loveballads, the robust and rollicking adventure
songs, the exuberant sea-chanteys, lumbsrmen's songs, soldiers' songs, with their
lusty uninhibited humor. The melodies he
sings range from the song of victory sung
by the conquering English soldiers after
the battle of Agincourt, to the "Waltzing
Matilda" sung by the Australian troops in
World War II. His repertoire is a sixcentuiy hit parade.
Songs of the growing pains of America,
hke "John Henry" which celebrates a
great
railroad man; comedy songs which might
be called 18th century "double talk," and
love songs of all the centuries fill out his
program.
With the hundred selections in German,
Swedish and French that the aged master
gave him, he returned to California to
begin another long journey. This was the
trip in search of recognition for an art
beloved by the people through centuries
devoid of r^adio, phonograph, concert hall,
in days when the wandering minstrel was
the welcome bearer of all the entertain
ment there was, as well as the only news
paper.
Richard Dyer-Bennet has proved his
point that the minstrel's art is undying.
Carnegie Hall in New York and the con
cert halls of major cities have shrunk to
living-room size imder the magic of his
new-old songs.
Bom in England, the son of a British
Army major, and listed in Burke's Peerage
as the descendant of one of England's
noble families. Brother Dyer-Bennet was
brought up in California and educated at
Berkeley. He was an
expert tennis and
soccer
player.
Dyer-Bennet went to Wales, where good
singing is traditional, and persuaded the
miners to listen to him. There was no
charge and the minstrel in the making was
merely getting good practice. His first

the People."

expect to turn out

period,
he believes that he can inculcate into his
charges the true principles of folk singing
and guitar playing.
Future plans also call for guest lectures
and performance by folk-art specialists of
various nations.

Has been elected president, for a second
term, of the Municipal Art Society, New
York City. Brother Keally is a fellow of the

were
present.
